comments.body:
Celebrities and performers should do what they do best: act, perform, sing, entertain, crack jokes... Whatever. Just do it and, otherwise, shut the hell up. 

They get into problems when they use their celebrity status to promote their own political, religious and philosophical views. 

They are generally not smarter than the rest of us and certainly, many are not intelligent at all, merely spouting popular "knee jerk" opinions that they picked up from uninformed sources.

I think Ricky Gervais said it best when he hosted the Golden Globe awards: 

"So, if you do win an award tonight, don't use it as a platform to make a political speech. You're in no position to lecture the public about anything. You know nothing about the real world. Most of you spent less time in school than Greta Thunberg. So if you win, come up, accept your little award, thank your agent and your god, and f— off."

comments.body:
When I was in early elementary school we read something about Israel and Egypt.  As a follow up assignment our teacher had us write a class letter to President Carter thanking him for helping “settle the Middle East War.” I vividly remember our excitement when we framed his “response” and hung it up in class. 

50 years later, i have learned that an American opining on who is right and who started what is a fool’s errand. But let’s all agree that killing people is wrong.

comments.name: Alfred F
comments.body:
What is happening to Israel and surrounding peoples is catastrophic and expected (not in the sense that is is deserved) and is going to continue and ramp up. If you don't believe this then you need to read more and read deeper.  It will not stop, others will be drawn into it, this is happening now.  Scary times for sure.

So entertainment is a way for us to divert ourselves from this crazy reality.

When anyone purchases a ticket to a concert, play, any ball game,  the expectation is that the event will follow what is customary for those particular performer(s).  Does any body expect an expression of the performers political or personal stance at intermission, half time, between songs, during 7th inning stretch, etc.  Of course not. It's just not what the average person agrees to when they buy a ticket.  It's not a question of freedom of speech, these performers can spread their personal thoughts through many other means but the purchased ticket and the attached event should not be one of them.  Eventually,  some hungary, savvy lawyers are going to pursue this abuse to force entertainers to stick to what is expected of them by the audience. 

We only want to hear what we paid for, we can chat about other stuff when the show is over, thank-you.

comments.name: JR
comments.body:
A deliberately laid out piece of writing. But reading this:
"Democrats should claim and occupy that mainstream, not lurch well out to the left, as they seem tempted to do."
Made me realize that the authors have not learned anything and really just want the Reagan era back.
It has been interesting to see how weak the Reagan era Republicans have been against MAGA.
What does "lurching to the left" even mean?
Americans want the rule of law but they also want much more equity and much much less concentration of wealth. We used to have public housing, very low cost public higher education, much less money in politics, and there was a time when FDR proposed universal health care. These are not "lurching to left" items. Many other civilized countries have these things and we want them in the USA now.

comments.body: This is a very optimistic reading of what Trump has succeeded and failed at. I would argue he has remade society to a far greater,  and longer lasting, extent than these authors write. Starting with making it acceptable to openly espouse racist beliefs.

comments.name: Kevin
comments.body:
The Trump administration is clearly preparing a big attack on the sorts of race-based policies favored by Democrats, timed for the 2028 election. This is why they’re not making deals with schools like Harvard. The key move will be to remove race entirely from the 2030 census. If a Republican is elected I bet this sticks. 

This question of whether Trump is a reactionary is complicated. When Trump is strong on an issue it’s usually because the Democrats have staked themselves on something unpopular, with them happening during Obama’s second term or later. They consider the issue a moral litmus test, or a defense of allies, and so they find it difficult to engage. 

The 2028 election is going to be fascinating, because we’re going to have fresh faces making sense of this. But who knows if the Democrats will stake out any position on contentious issues such as immigration. And without a strong vision I bet the election is a coin flip. Polls show the Democratic Party is still unpopular.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body:
This nicely recounts a small sampling of the destruction we have seen.  But it is too optimistic.  The United States most of us believe in is a thing of the past.  Unfortunately, with two years to go (also optimistic that this ends at that time) there will be little need to pretend that our foundational principles still exist.

What is really frightening, I think, is that this creature has dominated every waking moment for the last ten years.  Credence is given to his actions even by outlets that are critical by discussing him in terms of a legitimate actor.  Young people now coming into an understanding of the world around them have never known anything but him and opportunities for them to accurately learn what came before are assaulted hourly.  What will they work to go back to when they've seen nothing but this.

comments.name: jhead
comments.body: I wonder if the US is going to have to have something like the Truth and Reconciliation Commissions in South Africa, Argentina, and Chile after Trump is gone - he can't live forever - because someone will have to account for the crimes that were committed and the money that was stolen by him and his cronies while in office. On an even larger level, a moral majority is going to have to put laws in place to ensure that elections and officials can't be bought or coerced; that enforceable limits over executive power, particularly the powers of emergency and pardon, exist; that special interest groups and "black cabinet" appointees do not effectively control government; that all US citizens are taxed fairly and according to their income; and that immediate concerns like the environment and AI become the subject of federal policy and regulation against corporations that can't be expected to (fairly) measure their self-interest against the public good. I hope these measures appeal to people's sense of the common good, regardless of what political persuasion they claim.

articles.title: Refineries Are Now the Main Chokepoint for Global Energy Supplies
articles.summary: The Iran and Ukraine wars have exposed the world’s reliance on the Middle East and Russia for diesel.

I was born in the oil patch!

comments.name: Alex Stanley
comments.body:
Reading the comments, I can’t believe that at a time like this, we aren’t standing behind our president. Was the attack on Iran a bad idea? Yes - if there had been no reason for it. But there was a clear stated objective to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

The reason this escalated into such a clusterfunk, in my view, is that drone warfare has significantly changed modern warfare, suddenly giving countries and armed groups capabilities to project power far beyond their traditional regions. Blaming Trump alone for everything that followed seems unfair to me. I believe he genuinely thinks he is acting in what he sees as America’s best interests.

comments.name: Edda Kuhlmann
comments.body:
According to the IEA, before the war, Russia was the world’s largest exporter of oil to global markets and the second largest crude oil exporter behind Saudi Arabia. 

When the war started, Saudi Arabia et al picked up part of Russia's market shares.  Having alternatives kept the price relatively low. Now the alternatives are disrupted, too, markets are getting jittery. 

Blaming only Trump is dishonest. The days of factual reporting are clearly over.

Phase One of the Sturgeon Refinery is designed to process approximately 79,000 barrels per day of diluted bitumen from Alberta’s oil sands into much higher value products. This includes ultra-low sulphur diesel, vacuum gas oil, diluent, and natural gas liquids.

Refineries come at a high cost, hense the lack of costruction of new capacity in North America.

comments.name: David
comments.body:
There is a regulation that can be imposed on AI with relatively little effort but lots of impact.

Today, It is still true that every AI agent -- including those that launch other agents -- has a human "parent" -- the living, breathing human who made a conscious decision to click a button that said "LAUNCH", giving birth to the agent.

That human owner's identity should be recorded in a "Agent Birth Certificate" embedded into the agent (and its children) in a standard, cryptographically tamper-proof way.  Then, any computer system asked to provide access or support for the agent should be able to inspect this information, analyze it, contact the owner, or -- if the information is missing or invalid -- deem the agent hostile, deny resources to it, and stop it dead.

Intermediaries and services would spring up to help anyone identify the parent of an agent and decide whether to trust it.

There is still time to mandate that every AI agent be attached to a human (or corporation) at the other end -- the entity that would be strictly liable for any harm done to others by the agent or its children.

But as Ezra's piece suggests, once RSI arrives and AI is making and launching itself, it will be too late.

Or, establishing fines when an athlete continues in a competition when they know they’re about to release bodily fluids, and then do so on the course. comments.name: Michael Smith
comments.body:
I live in Australia. The sports culture here is extreme. It begins at a very young age and often involves a lot of bullying and cheating. Parents are heavily invested in their children’s future professional sporting success, and will engage in all sorts of unedifying behaviour on the sidelines. Living through one’s children is a vicarious form of narcissism, and it’s widespread.

I’m of South Asian extraction, and our equivalent of sporting hyper competition is academics. It is equally ruthless and no less damaging. I’ve seen individuals and families destroyed by the toxicity of constantly wanting to be seen as superior to everyone else.

In both endeavours, people are constantly learning how to play the system. They aren’t necessarily the best at what they do. I had to make a conscious effort not to repeat my parent’s mistakes when raising my son. This wasn’t easy as there’s no manual for that.

But I’m happy to report that it’s an approach that pays dividends - for parents and young people.

comments.body:
“The repellent images ... so outlandish and so viscerally off-putting ... a noxious mark on her road to victory ... Wietrzyk and Hyrox  ... made unconditional apologies ... Wietrzyk retroactively withdrew from the race...”

I agree with Ms. Grose that American sports culture is unhinged in important ways,  and that football is a glaring example. Brain damage is a real risk at all levels of tackle football, and it is shocking that the sport continues essentially unchanged.

The Hyrox incident is not comparable.

It is said that cleanliness is next to Godliness,  but it is possible to be too delicate.  Has Ms. Grose ever changed a diaper?  Ever had diarrhea?  Ever had a partner who had diarrhea?  Ever cleaned up after a neighbor’s dog?

Were there health or safety risks?  Did Ms. Wietrzyk interfere with her competitors?  Yes, but at a very minor level:  Some competitors reported that they had slipped on the damp spot. Apparently no one reported seeing contamination on shared equipment. Hyrox claims they have an “emergency response protocol for biological contamination incidents”, so things presumably got cleaned up.

Nothing here compares to the chronic traumatic encephalopathy or heat stroke cases Ms.Gross talks about.

Personally, I think that Ms. Wietrzyk was right to continue the race, and I congratulate her on her win.

comments.name: robin Perry
comments.body:
We bought our first home  in 2000 when I was 30 in Long Beach, CA. We moved to an area that looked as if its better days had come and gone. The housing stock was old but the neighborhood was walkable had good schools & was close to my office. When we purchased our home for 325,000, many thought we were crazy. Everyone, esspecially, older people, feared that it was too much for what we were getting. Fast-forward. 26 years The same neighborhood is one of the most desirable areas in our city and in fact in our region.. Our house has appreciated by a factor of 5.

I do fear that our adult children could not afford our home or nearly any home in Long Beach. The median price has climbed to almost least $900,000. That is a material change from what it wants was 25 years ago where two income families could buy a house in the region.

A solution is to live further and further away from the economic core. That has significant drawbacks including the commute, and access to economic and cultural opportunities..

The solution has to be building more homes, closer to the urban core and helping young people qualify with smaller down payments. . It’s easy to posit that  young adults are wasteful spenders with different priorities. But that just lets us off the hook for our failure to build sufficient housing like generations  before. “Slow growth”  has maintained  bucolic neighborhoods like mine while excluding the construction of apartments, townhomes, & condominiums that we need.

College or professional, no trips to gamble in Vegas, kept a used car at least 7-10 more years ( i worked in them, oil, filters, brakes, plugs,

When I did get my first home, I did all the maintenance, the exterior and interior painting, lawn, minor concrete work.  Did my own maintenance on HVAC, still worked on my car.  

Guess what?  It all paid off. I can now do want I want, when I want and take a vacation wherever I want to go.

The necklace story: I was wondering if the woman who gave the necklace to the MD story teller may have been from another culture?

My husband professor traveled the world for about 15 years, because our area of research (the development of "youth," roughly ages 18-30) is often of greater interest to other countries than in our country). 

In a couple of his early trips abroad--often to developing nations--he was unfamiliar with a country's customs. One time he was in the Middle East and complimented a man on his tie at a conference. The man took off the tie and gave to husband. 

Husband felt embarrassed, tried to give it back, but the man seemed genuinely upset and refused to take it back. A few years later, it happened again when husband complimented a man on a pouch he was carrying, so the man gives him the pouch. 

Then husband saw the cultural pattern--that giving someone a compliment may obligate them to show their generosity (seemingly happy to do so). Lovely custom.

Husband was traveling in a hot, humid country and someone from an African country at a conference complimented him on his LL Bean madras shirt. So husband took it off and gave it to him; and the fellow seemed quite delighted and remained friendly throughout the conference. 

Somewhere in between, husband learned to take an assortment of little gifts to give others on his trips.

Husband is 91. We have moved 3 times since we retired, and some of those gifts (esp. the lovely necktie) move with us.

That said, the item of clothing I get the greatest number of compliments about is a coat I received from a dear relative who sewed it more than 50 years ago now.

It is a beautiful corduroy, multi-colored patchwork coat, knee length, and fully lined with satin. I've even had a few women ask if they might buy it from me! If it weren't from a relative, I might consider being a bit more generous, but this is one item of clothing I'll never part with.

This relative, a step-great-aunt, to be precise, was one of those older relatives all kids should have. This was Aunt Blanche. Understanding, able to soothe all the hurts that come with childhood, and yet requiring the highest of standards in any undertaking. 

Oh, and she did have a quirky sense of humor. One of her grandchildren and I were the only two kids in any branch of her family who were quite studious. We were also the "odd kids out" because I was "only" step-family, and he was adopted. Because of this, she often said of me and of this grandchild that the smartest two people in their family weren't related to them.....

I had asked her years ago why she became a nurse, and she said because when she was four-years-old sitting in the waiting room waiting for her sister Diane to arrive, a nice nurse gave her an orange. 

Our eight-year-old grandson, Killian, came to visit this summer. As we drove through Flagstaff, AZ, he wanted to play the game of counting certain colors of cars. First it was blue cars, which we saw a lot. Then green cars. I told him about my unique connection with his great grandma through the color of orange, so let’s look for orange cars. He said that’d be hard because there aren’t many orange cars. So I said let’s spot two orange cars so we know it’s a sign from my mom and not a coincidence.

We saw no orange cars on our way to a large sporting goods store to buy fishing gear. In the back of the store was a wall display of small Hot Wheel’s-like cars and trucks. ‘Hey, Pappy, check it out.” He pointed to the middle of the display where two orange muscle cars sat side-by-side. I said well there’ s our sign, and I bought him one of the cars. I asked, “Are you ready to go?” And Killian responded, “Okey dokey.”

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: A fascinating article. What the author is addressing is an area called phenomenology—the field in Continental philosophy developed by Edmund Husserl in the early 20th century and advanced by others in philosophy, psychology and related disciplines. It’s a fancy word that means the study of phenomena—literally, that which appears. And what appears is mutually constituted by the “thing out there” and by our minds. One brackets or puts aside the question of “what is really existing” and focuses instead on the experience of what appears in consciousness. To me it seems that this would be a great research topic for neuroscience and cognitive science to work on together with phenomenology. I’m a pretty hardcore Logical Positivist day to day, but there are too many experiences like this to go unexamined. The experience is real, even if we cannot verify/falsify the persistence of life after death. The mention of  William James is especially relevant since he addresses both religious experience and the nature of belief in his major writings. It seems to me there is a cultural component here too—that people within different cultures might process these events differently—or similarly!

When my husband died in 2020, just nine months after his cancer diagnosis, I had no idea that everything I thought I knew about myself and the world was about to be turned upside down.

His death—and the extraordinary experiences that followed—did more than help me survive my grief. They opened something in me and allowed me to heal parts of myself I had shuttered long ago. I had always been an open-minded skeptic about the paranormal. Eventually, what I was experiencing became too difficult for me to dismiss.

For a long time, I desperately wanted other people to believe me. If they believed me, perhaps that made it real. Perhaps it meant he wasn't really gone.

I don't need that anymore.

At 59, I am stronger and healthier than I have ever been. I have come to believe there is far more to this world than what we can perceive with our five senses. I believe I will be with my husband again when my soul leaves this temporary form.

Most of all, I no longer fear death. His death, as devastating as it was, changed my understanding of what death is. I now see it as an awakening into what we have been all along: pure love, pure energy.

Companies that provide for betting such as Polymarket are indeed vulnerable to fraud. Even with regulation and good business practices this may be hard to prevent.

 

The greater risk is that they are vulnerable to insider trading and market manipulation. I don't see how these risks can be effectively managed. There is a substantial risk that those with implicit or explicit insider information may make wagers benefiting themselves at the expense of honest participants. The greater and more consequential risk is probably market manipulation, whereas those with the ability to influence outcomes may attempt to do so. This could happen in financial markets; perhaps the greater danger is that it could occur in situations that affect public policy, or even military situations. I don't stay awake at night worrying that adults may lose money to insider trading; as the saying goes, fools and their money are soon parted. I do worry about market manipulation that may have much wider effect.

 

I do not believe prediction markets such as Polyymarket serve a useful societal function.  I believe they should be outlawed in this country, or at the very least heavily regulated and appropriately taxed.

 

I also believe it is inappropriate for Dow Jones to have a contractual relationship with Polymarket. Though the reporting in this article seems thorough and impartial, I believe the relationship undermines the reputation and impartiality of the Journal.

The housing slump for example: A tremendous bubble that the government determined needed popping, which caused a much-needed slump in a grossly overpriced housing system where most purchases were not for living, but for investment.  And most signs indicate that despite the magnitude of the problem, China is emerging from it.  

There are plenty of tools in Mr. Xi's toolbox that he can employ if he wishes. The one cited by many economists is increased pensions, greater health care, or some other form of welfare.  Yet, in seeming contradiction of the praxis of a "People's" nation, Mr. Xi is loath to provide handouts.  Like traditional US Republicans, he believes that giveaways lead to moral turpitude, that the people should rise up by tugging on their own bootstraps.  This notion stretches back into dynastic China, and my residency in the country indicates that many people still believe in it. 

   Problems must be addressed, but it is also important to recognize that China bashing and jeremiads often cover up deep-seated schadenfreude.  Every nation has economic problems of one sort or another.  In analyzing China's faults, it is instructive to also look at those in the US.

comments.name: Lorna McGowan-Smith
comments.body: A fine and now saved (will I ever find it again?) piece, Sam Anderson. I have followed Annie Dillard since we were young women - she on the staff of Western Washington (then State College/now University) and I a young woman living in Bellingham trying to find out who I was. Her writing in turn baffled and charmed me, creating hit and run attempts on my part to tame it. Annie’s work was never to be tamed, at least by me.  At her passing I have returned to my fascination with her gifts and doff my hat to you, sir. Your essay made my day and much more.

comments.name: Todd Telford

Sam, thank you for sharing Annie's unique and vibrantly alive perspective on simple moments. Her imagination was - no as you insist is - like a sparkler held at half arm's distance: breathtaking yet dangerous, drawing you into a spell that you know will linger after the fuel is exhausted, albeit stripped of its promise of fresh discovery.

So you savor each moment of brilliance and unexpected clarity, knowing that part of the fun is taking the time to embrace and discern the unique wildness of each phrase.

Thank you again, Sam, for capturing the true impact of a legend.

comments.name: KateD
comments.body:
Exceptional tribute. Thank you. I agree that she lives forever in us. I read her astonishing “Total Eclipse” as a prelude to seeing the 2017 Total Eclipse in Oregon, my first. Being in Totality for nearly a minute changed my life as did the essay. 

The line: “We were born and bored at a stroke” seems a perfect synopsis of life as a Dillard reader.

comments.name: Erika
comments.body:
Thank you for this. Holy the Firm and The Maytrees are two of my favorite books of all time. Her sentences were poems, their rhythms like dance. There’s a passage in the Maytrees where the stoic, bookish main character reflects on the great love she has for her son as he is about to head off into his own adult life. She describes setting a table for each of the various iterations of him over the years. She knows each of him so well — his favorite foods, his moods, his habits. They are, each of him, fully whole separate people. It’s a passage that comes to mind every time I or someone close to me have lost someone we loved. Somehow the pain of their absence is eased just a little by that crowded table full of them; all the years and experiences of them now gathered together for us. 

And now each place at the table seats another of her beautiful books and essays, alive and immediate, timeless and ready to greet us like a Puget Sound day. Newborn and salted, the day’s god “…flings his arms, spreading colors; he arches, cupping sky in his belly; he vaults, vaulting and spread, holding all and spread on me like skin.”

The most useless international body on the planet, right up there with the ICC. Lots of bloviating, and then Russia and China blow everything apart if they try to do anything with the Security Council.
Love the idea of the UN, but if the US can't get along with Canada or NATO, and there is no effective military arm of the UN, who's to believe this body will be more than just hot air symbolizing nothing?

comments.name: Lea Lane
comments.body: My late husband Rabbi Chaim Stern edited the prayer book Gates of Repentance, still used in some services. In 2001, suffering from a terminal brain tumor, he summoned his strength to lead the Neilah service. I still remember the power of the prayers and how I contemplated our brief lives In the fading light of the temple. He died a few weeks later, comforted that he accomplished this moment in time as it has been shared through the ages..

comments.name: Francesca Regalado
comments.body:
Many myths are told in the Philippines about the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant — people say it was built directly above a fault line, there are cracks in the reactor structure, or that its waste will leak into the sea and nearby rice fields.

I wanted to see the plant for myself, as the government considers switching it on after mothballing it for 40 years. I also spent three days in the town of Morong, which has once again found itself at the center of the country's debate over nuclear power.

articles.title: An Unused and Divisive Philippine Nuclear Plant Awaits Its Fate
articles.summary: The government is exploring nuclear power options to guard against global energy shocks. One proposal is to switch on a plant in Bataan that has been mothballed for 40 years.
